title: 10. Exercises: File Handling Masterclass
summary: CONGRATULATIONS — You now have Complete Python File Handling Mastery!
objectives: Solve the File Handling Masterclass exercises without looking at the lesson
Test edge cases and explain your approach

sections.title: File Handling Basics — Coding Challenges (Chapter 1)
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
  Build a "File Inspector" tool that:
  - Takes a filepath as input
  - Reports: size, creation time, modification time, line count,
    word count, character count, encoding detection
  - Shows first and last 5 lines
  - Detects if file is text or binary
  - Shows file permissions (read/write/execute)

CHALLENGE 2:
  Create a "Safe File Backup" system:
  - Before any write operation, auto-backup original file
  - Backup with timestamp: file.txt → file.txt.2024-01-15_14:30:00.bak
  - Keep only last N backups (configurable)
  - Support restore from any backup
  - Log all backup/restore operations

CHALLENGE 3:
  Implement a "File Diff Tool":
  - Compare two text files line by line
  - Show: lines only in file1, lines only in file2, changed lines
  - Generate a diff report similar to Unix diff command
  - Support: ignore case, ignore whitespace options
  - Output: unified diff format

CHALLENGE 4:
  Build a "Multi-File Search Engine":
  - Given a directory and search term
  - Search all .txt files recursively
  - Return: filename, line number, line content for each match
  - Support: regex patterns, case-insensitive
  - Rank results by relevance (number of matches)

CHALLENGE 5:
  Write a "File Merger" utility:
  - Merge multiple text files into one
  - Options: with/without headers, separator between files
  - Handle different encodings (auto-detect and convert all to UTF-8)
  - Remove duplicate lines across all files
  - Generate merge report

CHALLENGE 6:
  Create a "File Split" utility:
  - Split large file into chunks of N lines or N bytes
  - Maintain header row in each chunk (for CSV-like files)
  - Name chunks: original_part001.txt, original_part002.txt
  - Support reassembly of split files
  - Progress reporting for large files

CHALLENGE 7:
  Build a "File Watcher Service":
  - Monitor a directory for file changes
  - Detect: new files, deleted files, modified files
  - Use polling with configurable interval
  - Callback functions for each event type
  - Maintain a state file to persist between restarts
  - Log all events with timestamp
```

sections.title: Reading & Writing Text Files — Coding Challenges (Chapters 2 & 3)
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
  Build a "Word Frequency Analyzer":
  - Read a large text file (or multiple files)
  - Count frequency of every word (case-insensitive)
  - Ignore stop words (the, a, an, in, on, etc.)
  - Handle punctuation (don't count "hello," as different from "hello")
  - Write results to output file: sorted by frequency (descending)
  - Include: word, count, percentage of total words
  - Top 10 words with visual bar chart (using # characters)

CHALLENGE 2:
  Create a "Smart File Splitter and Joiner":
  - Split a large text file into N equal parts (by lines)
  - Preserve header row in each part (for data files)
  - Smart split: don't break in middle of a "record" (detect by blank lines)
  - Join: reassemble in correct order from numbered parts
  - Verify integrity after join (line count matches original)

CHALLENGE 3:
  Implement a "File Diff and Patch" system:
  - Compare original and modified text files
  - Generate a patch file describing the differences
  - Apply patch file to original to regenerate modified
  - Support: add lines, delete lines, change lines
  - Format similar to Unix patch format
  - Verify patch application is correct

CHALLENGE 4:
  Write a "Log File Rotator":
  - Write to a log file
  - When file reaches N bytes, rotate: rename to .1, .2, etc.
  - Keep only last M rotated files (delete older ones)
  - New file starts fresh after rotation
  - Thread-safe rotation (handle concurrent writes)
  - Compression of rotated files (optional)

CHALLENGE 5:
  Build a "Multi-Language File Encoder/Decoder":
  - Read files with unknown encoding (auto-detect using chardet or BOM)
  - Convert between encodings: UTF-8, UTF-16, Latin-1, CP1252
  - Handle partial read failures gracefully
  - Report: original encoding, characters changed, conversion errors
  - Batch convert all files in a directory

CHALLENGE 6:
  Create a "Template-Based Report Generator":
  - Define report templates in text files with {{variables}}
  - Support: loops {{#for item in items}}...{{/for}}
  - Support: conditionals {{#if condition}}...{{/if}}
  - Load data from a JSON file
  - Render multiple reports from same template with different data
  - Save each report to a separate dated file

CHALLENGE 7:
  Build a "File-Based Database" (simplified):
  - Store records as one JSON object per line (JSONL)
  - Operations: insert, find (by field), update, delete
  - Support: filtering (multiple conditions), sorting, pagination
  - Index: maintain sorted index file for fast lookups
  - Transaction: write to temp, then atomic rename
  - Backup: keep last 3 versions of the data file
```

sections.title: OS Module — Complete Guide — Coding Challenges (Chapter 5 — OS Module)
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
  Build a "File System Monitor":
  - Watch a directory for changes (new, deleted, modified files)
  - Use polling with os.stat() to detect modifications
  - Track: file additions, deletions, renames, content changes
  - Generate events with timestamp and details
  - Persist state between runs (save last-known state to JSON)
  - Alert on suspicious patterns (many files deleted at once)

CHALLENGE 2:
  Create a "Smart Directory Cleaner":
  - Scan directory for: temp files, cache files, log files, duplicates
  - Categorize by: age, size, type, access frequency
  - Calculate space that would be freed
  - Support: dry-run, interactive (confirm each), batch mode
  - Generate before/after report
  - Undo support: log all deletions so they can be reversed

CHALLENGE 3:
  Implement a "File Indexer and Search Engine":
  - Recursively index all files in a directory tree
  - Build index: filename → (path, size, modified, hash)
  - Save index to JSON file for persistence
  - Search by: name pattern, extension, date range, size range
  - Update index incrementally (only re-scan changed files)
  - Show search results with relevance ranking

CHALLENGE 4:
  Write a "Directory Comparison Tool":
  - Compare two directories recursively
  - Find: files only in A, files only in B, files in both
  - For files in both: compare by size, date, content hash
  - Generate detailed diff report
  - Support: ignore patterns (.git, __pycache__), size threshold
  - Output: HTML report with colored diff

CHALLENGE 5:
  Build a "Disk Usage Analyzer" (like ncdu/du):
  - Calculate size of every directory recursively
  - Show percentage of parent directory
  - Visual bar charts using terminal characters
  - Top 10 largest files and directories
  - Group by file type with total sizes
  - Export report to CSV

CHALLENGE 6:
  Create a "Project Template Generator":
  - Define project templates in JSON config files
  - Templates specify: directory structure, files with content
  - Support: variable substitution {{project_name}}, {{author}}
  - Post-creation hooks (run commands after creation)
  - Multiple templates: web, cli, data-science, microservice
  - Validate created structure matches template spec

CHALLENGE 7:
  Implement a "File Permission Auditor" (Unix systems):
  - Scan directory for permission issues
  - Find: world-writable files, SUID/SGID bits, symlinks
  - Check: files owned by different users, group mismatches
  - Generate security report with risk levels
  - Fix permissions automatically (with dry-run mode)
  - Compare permissions against a "known good" baseline
```

sections.title: CSV Files — Complete Guide — Coding Challenges (Chapter 7 — CSV)
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
  Build a "CSV Schema Validator":
  - Define schema: required columns, types, regex patterns, ranges
  - Validate any CSV file against the schema
  - Report: missing columns, type errors, pattern mismatches
  - Line-by-line validation with error count per column
  - Generate a validation report CSV with pass/fail per row

CHALLENGE 2:
  Create a "CSV Pivot Table Generator":
  - Read any CSV file
  - Let user specify: row dimension, column dimension, value, aggregation
  - Aggregations: sum, count, average, min, max
  - Output result as formatted CSV
  - Handle missing values and non-numeric data gracefully

CHALLENGE 3:
  Write a "CSV Deduplication Tool":
  - Find duplicate rows based on specified key columns
  - Strategies: keep first, keep last, keep with highest value in a field
  - Handle case-insensitive duplicates (ALICE = alice = Alice)
  - Report: duplicate groups, rows removed, rows kept
  - Output: clean CSV and duplicate report CSV

CHALLENGE 4:
  Build a "Multi-CSV Merger":
  - Merge multiple CSV files with same or similar schemas
  - Handle mismatched columns (fill with empty or default values)
  - Track source file for each row
  - Support: inner join, outer join on key column
  - Deduplicate after merge based on key
  - Generate merge statistics report

CHALLENGE 5:
  Implement a "CSV Statistics Analyzer":
  - For each column: type detection, unique count, null count
  - For numeric columns: min, max, mean, median, std dev, percentiles
  - For string columns: min/max length, most common values, pattern detection
  - Detect outliers (values > 3 std devs from mean)
  - Generate HTML report with statistics and basic charts (ASCII)

CHALLENGE 6:
  Create a "CSV Time Series Processor":
  - CSV with date column and numeric value columns
  - Calculate: rolling average, cumulative sum, period-over-period change
  - Resample: daily → weekly → monthly aggregations
  - Fill missing dates with interpolated values
  - Detect anomalies (values outside expected range)
  - Export processed time series to new CSV

CHALLENGE 7:
  Build a "CSV API Mock Server":
  - Load data from CSV files
  - Expose REST-like interface (as functions):
    GET(table, filters, sort, page, page_size)
    POST(table, record) → insert row
    PUT(table, key, updates) → update row
    DELETE(table, key) → mark row as deleted
  - Persist changes back to CSV files
  - Support: multiple CSV files as "tables"
  - Transaction support: rollback on error
```

sections.title: JSON Files — Complete Guide — Coding Challenges (Chapter 8 — JSON)
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
  Build a "JSON Schema Validator":
  - Define schema in JSON: required fields, types, constraints
  - Validate any JSON document against the schema
  - Support: nested objects, arrays, enum values, regex patterns
  - Generate helpful error messages with JSON path (e.g., "data.users[2].email")
  - Support: optional fields, nullable fields, custom validators

CHALLENGE 2:
  Create a "JSON Config Hot-Reload System":
  - Watch config.json file for changes (use os.stat mtime)
  - Automatically reload when file changes
  - Validate new config before applying (don't apply invalid config)
  - Notify registered callbacks when specific keys change
  - Keep old config as fallback if new config is invalid
  - Log all config changes with timestamp and what changed

CHALLENGE 3:
  Implement a "JSON Data Transformer":
  - Read JSON, apply transformation rules defined in another JSON
  - Rules: rename keys, delete keys, add computed fields
  - Rules: type conversion, string formatting, conditional transforms
  - Support: nested transforms, array element transforms
  - Output transformed JSON with transformation report

CHALLENGE 4:
  Write a "JSON Diff Tool":
  - Compare two JSON files/objects
  - Find: added keys, deleted keys, changed values
  - Support: nested objects, arrays (by index and by content)
  - Output diff in human-readable format and machine-readable format
  - Generate patch JSON that transforms doc1 into doc2
  - Apply patch to verify it produces doc2

CHALLENGE 5:
  Build a "JSON API Mock Server" (functions only, no network):
  - Define API endpoints and responses in JSON config files
  - Support: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE methods
  - Dynamic responses: use request data in response templates
  - State management: POST updates state, GET reads state
  - Persist state to JSON file between calls
  - Response delays simulation, error rate simulation

CHALLENGE 6:
  Create a "JSON Data Aggregator":
  - Process a large JSONL file with user events
  - Aggregate: events per user, events per hour, funnel analysis
  - Group by: multiple dimensions simultaneously
  - Calculate: counts, sums, averages, unique counts
  - Output: aggregated results as JSON and CSV
  - Handle: missing fields, null values, type mismatches

CHALLENGE 7:
  Build a "JSON-based ORM" (simplified):
  - Store "tables" as JSON files (one file per table)
  - Operations: create, read, update, delete, find, filter
  - Relationships: foreign key references between tables
  - Indexes: maintain sorted index files for fast queries
  - Transactions: write to temp then atomic rename
  - Migrations: schema version tracking and upgrade scripts
```

sections.title: Log Files — Complete Guide — Coding Challenges (Chapter 10 — Logging)
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
  Build a "Log Aggregator and Analyzer":
  - Parse log files from multiple services (different formats)
  - Normalize to standard format: timestamp, level, service, message
  - Generate: error rate by service, errors per hour chart
  - Find: error spikes (sudden increase in error rate)
  - Alert rules: "more than 10 errors in 5 minutes from same service"
  - Output: aggregated JSONL and HTML report

CHALLENGE 2:
```

```

CHALLENGE 2:
Create a "Structured Logging Framework":

- Custom Logger class with JSON output
- Context manager for request/transaction tracing
- Automatic correlation ID generation and propagation
- Performance timing: log duration of any code block
- Sampling: log only X% of DEBUG messages (reduce noise)
- Sensitive data masking: auto-redact passwords, tokens, card numbers

CHALLENGE 3:
Implement a "Log-Based Alerting System":

- Watch log files for patterns in real-time (tail -f style)
- Define alert rules in JSON config:
  {"pattern": "ERROR", "threshold": 5, "window_seconds": 60}
- Alert channels: write to alert.log, send to console
- Cooldown period: don't re-alert for same issue within N minutes
- Alert severity levels: warning vs critical thresholds
- Track alert history and resolution

CHALLENGE 4:
Build a "Log Rotation and Archival System":

- Rotate logs: by size (10MB), by time (daily), or both
- Compress rotated logs (gzip)
- Archive old logs to a separate directory
- Delete archives older than N days
- Maintain a rotation manifest (JSON): what was rotated, when, size
- Verify compressed archives are not corrupted after rotation

CHALLENGE 5:
Write a "Performance Profiling Logger":

- Decorator: @log_performance to time any function
- Context manager: with log_timing("operation_name"):
- Track: calls per function, avg/min/max duration, p95/p99
- Detect slow functions: alert if duration > threshold
- Generate performance report: sorted by total time consumed
- Save profiling data to JSON for trend analysis

CHALLENGE 6:
Create a "Audit Trail System":

- Log every data change: who, what, when, before value, after value
- Tamper detection: each log entry includes hash of previous entry
- Verify integrity: check hash chain is unbroken
- Search audit trail: by user, date range, resource, action
- Export audit trail to CSV for compliance reports
- Immutable logs: append-only, prevent modification of old entries

CHALLENGE 7:
Build a "Multi-Service Log Correlation Tool":

- Each service writes logs with correlation_id header
- Given a correlation_id, find ALL related log entries across ALL service log files
- Reconstruct full request timeline across services
- Identify bottlenecks: which service took the most time
- Find error propagation: which service error caused downstream failures
- Output: timeline visualization using ASCII art

```

sections.title: Error Handling in File Operations — Coding Challenges (Chapter 11 — Error Handling)
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
  Build a "Resilient File Processor":
  - Process files from a directory with comprehensive error handling
  - Each file gets up to 3 retry attempts with exponential backoff
  - Categorize errors: transient (retry) vs permanent (skip)
  - Maintain a "dead letter queue" for permanently failed files
  - Generate error report: error type frequency, file paths, messages
  - Continue processing remaining files even if one fails

CHALLENGE 2:
  Create a "File System Health Checker":
  - Check: disk space, inode usage, file count limits
  - Verify: required directories exist, have correct permissions
  - Test: can create/read/write/delete files in each directory
  - Check: files older than N days (potential stale locks/temps)
  - Alert levels: OK, WARNING (>75%), CRITICAL (>90%)
  - Output: health report JSON with remediation suggestions

CHALLENGE 3:
  Implement a "Safe Config File Manager":
  - Read config file with validation against expected schema
  - On parse error: use last known good config (saved separately)
  - On missing keys: fill with defaults and log warnings
  - On write error: retry with exponential backoff, then abort
  - Keep history of 5 last valid configs for rollback
  - Never leave config in partially-written state (atomic writes)

CHALLENGE 4:
  Write a "File Operation Audit Logger":
  - Wrap all file operations (open, read, write, delete)
  - Log every operation: timestamp, operation, path, result, duration
  - Catch and log all exceptions without re-raising (for monitoring)
  - Calculate: success rate, average duration, error frequency
  - Alert if error rate exceeds threshold in sliding window
  - Export audit to CSV daily

CHALLENGE 5:
  Build a "Crash-Recovery File Processor":
  - Process large batches of files
  - Save checkpoint after every N files (which ones are done)
  - On restart: skip already-processed files (read checkpoint)
  - Handle: corrupted checkpoint file, missing checkpoint
  - Support: graceful shutdown (Ctrl+C saves checkpoint first)
  - Report: total processed, resumed from checkpoint, newly processed

CHALLENGE 6:
  Create a "Multi-Format File Reader" with graceful degradation:
  - Try to read file as JSON, then CSV, then YAML, then plain text
  - Each format tried in order until one succeeds
  - For each failure: log why it failed (parse error, encoding, etc.)
  - Return parsed data in normalized dict format regardless of source format
  - Handle encoding detection automatically
  - Report: which format succeeded, conversion warnings

CHALLENGE 7:
  Implement a "File Transaction System":
  - Group multiple file operations into a "transaction"
  - Before each operation: save backup of affected file
  - If ANY operation fails: rollback ALL previous operations
  - Support: create, update, delete, rename within a transaction
  - Concurrent safety: lock files during transaction
  - Nested transactions: support savepoints for partial rollback
```

╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║  READING                                                                  ║
║  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ║

║  f.readlines()       → all lines as LIST                                 ║

║  f.flush()           → force buffer to disk NOW                          ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣

║  Pattern:                                                                 ║
║  try:                                                                     ║
║      with open(path) as f: ...                                           ║
║  except FileNotFoundError: ...   ← specific first                       ║
║  except PermissionError: ...                                              ║
║  except OSError as e: ...        ← catch-all for rest                   ║
║  else: ...                       ← only if NO exception                  ║
║  finally: ...                    ← ALWAYS runs (cleanup)                 ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║  GOLDEN RULES (5 Years Experience)                                        ║
║  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ║
║  1. ALWAYS use 'with' statement — never manual close()                   ║
║  2. ALWAYS specify encoding='utf-8' explicitly                           ║
║  3. ALWAYS use newline='' for CSV files                                  ║
║  4. NEVER use 'w' mode without being sure you want to overwrite          ║
║  5. ALWAYS prefer for-loop over read() for large files                   ║
║  6. ALWAYS use DictReader/DictWriter over reader/writer                  ║
║  7. ALWAYS use named loggers, never root logger in libraries             ║
║  8. ALWAYS catch specific exceptions before generic OSError              ║
║  9. ALWAYS use atomic writes for critical data (temp → rename)           ║
║  10. ALWAYS test with dry_run=True before destructive file operations    ║

# 🔥 TOP 25 FILE HANDLING INTERVIEW QUESTIONS — QUICK FIRE

```
Q: Why use 'with' instead of open/close?
A: Auto-closes even on exception. Prevents file descriptor leaks.

Q: What does mode 'w' do to existing file content?
A: DELETES it completely (truncates to zero). Use 'a' to preserve!

Q: Why specify encoding='utf-8' explicitly?
A: Default encoding varies by OS. Explicit = portable, consistent.

Q: How to read large files without filling RAM?
A: for line in f: — Python's iterator reads one line at a time.

Q: newline='' in csv.open() — why?
A: Prevents double newline processing (Python + csv both handle it).

Q: DictReader vs reader — which to use?
A: Always DictReader — column names make code readable and robust.

Q: json.load() vs json.loads() difference?
A: load() reads from FILE object; loads() parses a STRING.

Q: What Python types are NOT JSON serializable?
A: datetime, Decimal, set, bytes, UUID, custom classes.

Q: How to pretty-print JSON?
A: json.dumps(data, indent=4, sort_keys=True)

Q: What is JSONL format?
A: One JSON object per line. Streamable, appendable, grep-able.

Q: os.mkdir() vs os.makedirs() difference?
A: mkdir creates ONE dir; makedirs creates ALL intermediate dirs.

Q: os.remove() vs shutil.rmtree() difference?
A: remove() = single file; rmtree() = directory + all contents.

Q: os.rename() vs shutil.move() difference?
A: rename() = same filesystem only; move() = across filesystems.

Q: How to get file size in bytes?
A: os.path.getsize(filepath) or filepath.stat().st_size (pathlib)

Q: How to find all files recursively?
A: os.walk() or Path.rglob('*') for all, rglob('*.py') by pattern

Q: FileNotFoundError vs OSError?
A: FileNotFoundError IS an OSError (subclass). Catch specific first!

Q: logger.error() vs logger.exception()?
A: exception() adds full traceback. Use in except blocks always!

Q: What is RotatingFileHandler?
A: Splits log file at size limit. Keeps N backup copies automatically.

Q: How to make file writes crash-safe?
A: Write to temp file → os.replace(temp, target) = atomic swap.

Q: os.path vs pathlib.Path — which to use?
A: pathlib is modern (3.6+). Prefer it. os.path in legacy code.

Q: How to check if you can read/write a file?
A: os.access(path, os.R_OK) / os.access(path, os.W_OK)

Q: How to detect file encoding?
A: Check for BOM bytes. Or use chardet library for detection.

Q: What does f.flush() do?
A: Forces Python's write buffer to OS. Does NOT guarantee disk write.
   Use f.flush() + os.fsync(f.fileno()) for guarantee.

Q: How to process CSV with missing columns gracefully?
A: csv.DictReader with restval='N/A' for missing, extrasaction='ignore'

Q: Log level DEBUG vs INFO — production setting?
A: Production: INFO (hides debug noise). Development: DEBUG.
   Never DEBUG in high-traffic production (performance + log size).
```
